Part I · The Action Principle — Chapter 1.3

Hamilton and Phase Space

Trade nnn second-order equations for 2n2n2n first-order ones, and the geometry starts doing the work.

Where we are

Chapter 1.2 handed you a machine. Feed it one scalar function L(q,q˙,t)L(q,\dot q,t)L(q,q˙​,t) and it returns nnn second-order differential equations, one per degree of freedom, in a form that survives any change of coordinates you care to make. That machine is not going away. It is the formulation that generalises to special relativity (Chapter 2.5), to fields (Chapter 5.2), and to curved spacetime (Chapter 3.6), and the reason is that the action is a scalar. Scalars do not care what you call your coordinates.

This chapter builds a second machine out of the same materials. It costs one change of variables. We swap the velocities q˙i\dot q^{i}q˙​i for the momenta pi=∂L/∂q˙ip_{i}=\partial L/\partial\dot q^{i}pi​=∂L/∂q˙​i, and in exchange we get three things the Lagrangian formulation does not give us.

The first is 2n2n2n first-order equations in place of nnn second-order ones. That means the state of the system is a single point, and the dynamics is a flow.

The second is a theorem, Liouville's, saying that flow is incompressible. It is the foundation of statistical mechanics. Read correctly, it is also the classical ancestor of the statement that quantum evolution is unitary.

The third is the one to keep your eye on. It is an operation on functions called the Poisson bracket, and it has the property that

replacing it by 1iℏ[  ,  ]\dfrac{1}{\ii\hbar}\big[\;,\;\big]iℏ1​[,] and changing nothing else turns classical mechanics into quantum mechanics.

That is what Part I is for. Chapter 4.9 will spend one line doing the substitution and the rest of the chapter reaping it, and the reason that line can be short is that this chapter is long.

Here is the summary you should finish with. The Lagrangian formulation is the one that generalises; the Hamiltonian formulation is the one that quantises. You need both, for different reasons, and mistaking one for the other is a standard way to get stuck.

Tools you'll need  — Chapter 0.4: the determinant as a volume factor, the trace, and det⁡(I+ϵA)=1+ϵ trA+O(ϵ2)\det(I+\epsilon A)=1+\epsilon\,\mathrm{tr}A+O(\epsilon^{2})det(I+ϵA)=1+ϵtrA+O(ϵ2). Section 5 is that identity. Chapter 0.5: quadratic forms and positive definiteness, which is exactly the condition §1 needs. Chapter 0.6: the Hessian, convexity, the multivariable chain rule, and Clairaut's theorem on mixed partials. Sections 5, 6 and 7 each turn on Clairaut and nothing else. Chapter 0.7: divergence as the trace of the Jacobian, hence as the fractional rate of change of volume carried by a flow. Section 5 is one substitution into that result. Chapter 0.8: Picard–Lindelöf and the uniqueness of solutions, the harmonic oscillator, the phase-space ellipse, and the pendulum's separatrix. Chapter 1.2: Euler–Lagrange, the canonical momentum pi=∂L/∂q˙ip_{i}=\partial L/\partial\dot q^{i}pi​=∂L/∂q˙​i, and Problem 2's Beltrami identity, which, you are about to discover, was the Hamiltonian all along.

1 · The Legendre transform, properly

Chapter 1.2's Problem 2 asked you to show that when LLL has no explicit time dependence the quantity

E  =  q˙ ∂L∂q˙  −  L E \;=\; \dot q\,\pdv{L}{\dot q} \;-\; L E=q˙​∂q˙​∂L​−L (1.3.1)

is conserved. We are about to promote that combination from a conserved quantity to the central object of a whole formulation of mechanics. It will be a great deal less mysterious if you first see what kind of operation it is.

It is not an ad hoc grouping of terms. It is an instance of a standard construction with a clean geometric meaning, and the same construction is what turns the internal energy of a gas into its free energy. So here is the plan for this section: §1 is mathematics, and there is no mechanics in it at all.

1.1 · Two ways to describe a curve

Take a smooth, strictly convex function f:R→Rf:\R\to\Rf:R→R. For now just picture a parabola. There are two ways to say which function it is.

By points. List the pairs (x,f(x))\big(x,f(x)\big)(x,f(x)). This is the description you grew up with.

By tangent lines. For each slope ppp, there is exactly one line of that slope tangent to the graph. Give me the family of all those lines, meaning for each ppp its intercept, and I can reconstruct the curve. The reason is that a convex curve is the upper envelope of its own tangent lines. Every tangent line lies below the graph and touches it once, and the graph is what you get by taking, at each xxx, the highest of them.

Both descriptions contain the same information. The Legendre transform is the dictionary between them. That is the whole idea, and the formula is going to be an immediate consequence of it rather than a definition to memorise.

Let's set it up. A line of slope ppp has the form y=px−cy = px - cy=px−c, where −c-c−c is its yyy-intercept. We carry the minus sign because it makes every formula below come out with a plus.

Now push this line down from above, increasing ccc, until it first touches the graph. Touching means the vertical gap between line and graph has shrunk to zero somewhere. Before that moment the line sits above the graph everywhere. So the critical value of ccc is the largest gap there ever was, which we write as

g(p)  ≡  sup⁡x[ p x  −  f(x) ]. g(p) \;\equiv\; \sup_{x}\Big[\,p\,x \;-\; f(x)\,\Big]. g(p)≡xsup​[px−f(x)]. (1.3.2)

Read the bracket as: how far the line y=pxy=pxy=px rises above the graph at the point xxx. Take the largest such gap. That is the amount you must lower y=pxy=pxy=px to make it tangent, and it is therefore precisely −(intercept of the tangent line of slope p)-(\text{intercept of the tangent line of slope }p)−(intercept of the tangent line of slope p).

What ggg is, in one sentence

g(p)g(p)g(p) is minus the yyy-intercept of the tangent line to fff whose slope is ppp. The function ggg is the "by tangent lines" description of fff, packaged so that its argument is the slope.

Everything else in §1 is a consequence of that sentence: the formula p=f′(x)p=f'(x)p=f′(x), the involution g∗∗=fg^{**}=fg∗∗=f, the thermodynamic potentials, and H=pq˙−LH=p\dot q-LH=pq˙​−L.

1.2 · Where the supremum sits

Now let's do the calculus. The bracket in (1.3.2) is, for fixed ppp, an ordinary function of the single variable xxx. So we want its stationary point, and Chapter 0.6's rule for finding one applies without change:

∂∂x[px−f(x)]  =  p−f′(x)  =  0⟹  p=f′(x).   \pdv{}{x}\Big[px-f(x)\Big] \;=\; p - f'(x) \;=\; 0 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \boxed{\;p = f'(x).\;} ∂x∂​[px−f(x)]=p−f′(x)=0⟹p=f′(x).​ (1.3.3)

So the maximising xxx is the point where the graph's own slope equals ppp, which is exactly what "tangent line of slope ppp" meant. Nothing has been assumed yet except differentiability. Two questions remain, and they are what convexity is for.

Is the stationary point a maximum? The second derivative of the bracket is −f′′(x)-f''(x)−f′′(x), which is negative wherever f′′>0f''\gt0f′′>0. So yes, provided fff is strictly convex.

Is there exactly one? The equation f′(x)=pf'(x)=pf′(x)=p must have a unique solution for each ppp in range. Since f′′>0f''\gt0f′′>0 means f′f'f′ is strictly increasing, f′f'f′ is injective, and so it is invertible on its image. Again convexity, and again it is doing genuine work rather than decorating the theorem.

That unique maximiser is a function of ppp, so give it a name and write x(p)x(p)x(p). Substituting it back into the definition turns the supremum into an ordinary formula:

g(p)  =  p x(p)  −  f(x(p)),where f′(x(p))=p. g(p) \;=\; p\,x(p) \;-\; f\big(x(p)\big), \qquad\text{where } f'\big(x(p)\big)=p. g(p)=px(p)−f(x(p)),where f′(x(p))=p. (1.3.4)

Put (1.3.4) beside (1.3.1) and the shape is already the same: slope times variable, minus the function. We will make that identification precise in §2.

1.3 · The transform is its own inverse

Here is the property that makes the construction worth having, and getting it takes one differentiation. We want to know what ggg does when its own argument ppp changes, so differentiate (1.3.4) with respect to ppp, using the product rule and the chain rule:

dgdp  =  x(p)  +  p dxdp  −  f′(x(p)) dxdp  =  x(p), \dv{g}{p} \;=\; x(p) \;+\; p\,\dv{x}{p} \;-\; f'\big(x(p)\big)\,\dv{x}{p} \;=\; x(p), dpdg​=x(p)+pdpdx​−f′(x(p))dpdx​=x(p), (1.3.5)

The last two terms cancel exactly, because f′(x(p))=pf'(x(p))=pf′(x(p))=p. That cancellation is not a coincidence, and it will happen again in §3 for the same reason: we are differentiating at a stationary point, so the motion of the stationary point itself contributes nothing at first order.

Now set the result beside the equation that defined the maximiser in the first place. Reading (1.3.5) next to (1.3.3) gives

f′(x)=p,g′(p)=x. f'(x) = p, \qquad\qquad g'(p) = x. f′(x)=p,g′(p)=x. (1.3.6)

Perfectly symmetric. The transform swaps the roles of the variable and the slope. And since g′′(p)=dx/dp=1/f′′(x)>0g''(p) = \dd x/\dd p = 1/f''(x) \gt 0g′′(p)=dx/dp=1/f′′(x)>0, the transform of a strictly convex function is strictly convex, so we are entitled to transform a second time. Let's do exactly that and see where it lands:

g∗(x)  =  sup⁡p[xp−g(p)], g^{*}(x) \;=\; \sup_{p}\big[xp - g(p)\big], g∗(x)=psup​[xp−g(p)], (1.3.7)

Its supremum sits where g′(p)=xg'(p)=xg′(p)=x, which by (1.3.6) is the ppp with x(p)=xx(p)=xx(p)=x, which is p=f′(x)p=f'(x)p=f′(x). So evaluate the bracket there and see what number comes out:

g∗(x)  =  x f′(x)−[f′(x) x−f(x)]  =  f(x). g^{*}(x) \;=\; x\,f'(x) - \Big[f'(x)\,x - f(x)\Big] \;=\; f(x). g∗(x)=xf′(x)−[f′(x)x−f(x)]=f(x). (1.3.8)

The Legendre transform is an involution on strictly convex functions. Do it twice and you are back where you started. That is what "dictionary" meant. No information is lost going from the point description to the tangent-line description, because you can always go back.

⚑ One statement here is quoted rather than proved. For a function that is not convex, the transform still exists, since the supremum in (1.3.2) is well defined whenever it is finite. What fails is the involution. The double transform g∗g^{*}g∗ returns the convex hull of fff, meaning the largest convex function lying below it, and any non-convex wiggles are erased permanently. This is the Fenchel–Moreau theorem, and it is the precise sense in which "the tangent lines determine the curve" needs convexity. It matters because it tells us which Lagrangians the Hamiltonian formulation applies to, and we will need it for exactly that in §2.3.

1.4 · A worked scalar example

Abstract dictionaries are easier to trust once you have run one. Take f(x)=14x4f(x)=\tfrac14 x^{4}f(x)=41​x4 on x≥0x\ge0x≥0, which is strictly convex there (f′′=3x2>0f''=3x^{2}\gt0f′′=3x2>0 for x≠0x\neq0x=0). Then p=f′(x)=x3p = f'(x) = x^{3}p=f′(x)=x3, so x=p1/3x = p^{1/3}x=p1/3, and putting that into (1.3.4) gives

g(p)  =  p⋅p1/3−14(p1/3)4  =  p4/3−14p4/3  =  34 p4/3. g(p) \;=\; p\cdot p^{1/3} - \tfrac14\big(p^{1/3}\big)^{4} \;=\; p^{4/3} - \tfrac14 p^{4/3} \;=\; \tfrac34\,p^{4/3}. g(p)=p⋅p1/3−41​(p1/3)4=p4/3−41​p4/3=43​p4/3. (1.3.9)

Now check the involution on this example, without appealing to the theorem. First the inverse relation: g′(p)=34⋅43p1/3=p1/3=xg'(p) = \tfrac34\cdot\tfrac43 p^{1/3} = p^{1/3} = xg′(p)=43​⋅34​p1/3=p1/3=x ✓, matching (1.3.6). Then transform a second time and see whether fff comes back:

g∗(x)  =  sup⁡p[xp−34p4/3]atp=x3⟹x4−34x4=14x4=f(x).  ✓ g^{*}(x) \;=\; \sup_{p}\Big[xp - \tfrac34 p^{4/3}\Big] \quad\text{at}\quad p = x^{3} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad x^{4} - \tfrac34 x^{4} = \tfrac14 x^{4} = f(x). \;\checkmark g∗(x)=psup​[xp−43​p4/3]atp=x3⟹x4−43​x4=41​x4=f(x).✓ (1.3.10)

It does. And the supremum is a real number you can measure rather than a formal device. Numerically, at p=2p=2p=2 the supremum of 2x−14x42x-\tfrac14x^{4}2x−41​x4 over a fine grid is 1.88988161.88988161.8898816, and 34⋅24/3=1.8898816\tfrac34\cdot2^{4/3} = 1.889881643​⋅24/3=1.8898816. The formula is measuring something real.

Familiar ground

You have used this transform for years under a different name, and knowing that it is the same operation makes the zoo of thermodynamic potentials collapse into one idea.

Start from the internal energy U(S,V)U(S,V)U(S,V) of a simple system, whose differential is the first law,

dU  =  T dS  −  P dV,soT=∂U∂S∣V,P=−∂U∂V∣S. \dd U \;=\; T\,\dd S \;-\; P\,\dd V, \qquad\text{so}\qquad T = \pdv{U}{S}\bigg|_{V}, \quad P = -\pdv{U}{V}\bigg|_{S}. dU=TdS−PdV,soT=∂S∂U​​V​,P=−∂V∂U​​S​.

Look at what that says about temperature. Temperature is the slope of UUU with respect to entropy. Now suppose you would rather label states by TTT than by SSS, which is what a laboratory forces on you, since thermometers exist and entropy meters do not. That is exactly the swap (1.3.6) performs. So define

F(T,V)  =  U(S,V)−TSevaluated at the S where ∂U∂S=T, F(T,V) \;=\; U(S,V) - T S \qquad\text{evaluated at the } S \text{ where } \pdv{U}{S}=T, F(T,V)=U(S,V)−TSevaluated at the S where ∂S∂U​=T,

and the Helmholtz free energy is −1-1−1 times the Legendre transform of UUU in the variable SSS. (Physicists carry the extra minus sign so that FFF is minimised at equilibrium. The mathematical content is identical.) To see which variables FFF naturally belongs to, take its differential, which is one line:

dF=dU−T dS−S dT=−S dT−P dV, \dd F = \dd U - T\,\dd S - S\,\dd T = -S\,\dd T - P\,\dd V, dF=dU−TdS−SdT=−SdT−PdV,

The T dST\,\dd STdS terms cancel, and it is the same cancellation as (1.3.5), for the same reason. So the natural variables of FFF are (T,V)(T,V)(T,V), and S=−∂F/∂TS=-\partial F/\partial TS=−∂F/∂T is the inverse relation (1.3.6).

Every other potential is the same move on a different slot. Transform V→PV\to PV→P instead and you get the enthalpy H=U+PV\mathcal{H}=U+PVH=U+PV with dH=T dS+V dP\dd\mathcal{H}=T\,\dd S+V\,\dd PdH=TdS+VdP. Transform both and you get the Gibbs free energy G=H−TS=U−TS+PVG=\mathcal{H}-TS=U-TS+PVG=H−TS=U−TS+PV with dG=−S dT+V dP\dd G=-S\,\dd T+V\,\dd PdG=−SdT+VdP, which is why GGG is the one a chemist uses. Its natural variables are the two a bench can control.

Convexity is not decoration here either. The statement ∂2U/∂S2=∂T/∂S=T/CV>0\partial^{2}U/\partial S^{2} = \partial T/\partial S = T/C_{V} \gt 0∂2U/∂S2=∂T/∂S=T/CV​>0 is thermodynamic stability, and it is exactly the condition (1.3.3) needed for the transform to be invertible. So a system with negative heat capacity has no well-defined free energy. That is not a mathematical curiosity. Self-gravitating systems have exactly that pathology, and it is why a star heats up when it loses energy.

In §2 we do the identical operation on L(q,q˙)L(q,\dot q)L(q,q˙​), swapping q˙\dot qq˙​ for its slope p=∂L/∂q˙p=\partial L/\partial\dot qp=∂L/∂q˙​. Same transform, same cancellation, same inverse relation. Only the letters change.

Grind box — Young's inequality, and what the supremum is really enforcing

Definition (1.3.2) says g(p)≥px−f(x)g(p)\ge px-f(x)g(p)≥px−f(x) for every xxx, with equality only at the maximiser. Rearranged, that is

p x  ≤  f(x)+g(p)for all x,p, p\,x \;\le\; f(x) + g(p) \qquad\text{for all } x,p, px≤f(x)+g(p)for all x,p,

with equality precisely when p=f′(x)p=f'(x)p=f′(x). This is Young's inequality, and it is not a separate theorem. It is the definition of the transform, read sideways.

The classic case is f(x)=xa/af(x)=x^{a}/af(x)=xa/a with a>1a\gt1a>1 on x≥0x\ge0x≥0. Then p=xa−1p=x^{a-1}p=xa−1, so x=p1/(a−1)x=p^{1/(a-1)}x=p1/(a−1) and

g(p)=pa/(a−1)−1apa/(a−1)=a−1a pa/(a−1)=pbb,1a+1b=1, g(p) = p^{a/(a-1)} - \frac{1}{a}p^{a/(a-1)} = \frac{a-1}{a}\,p^{a/(a-1)} = \frac{p^{b}}{b}, \qquad \frac1a+\frac1b=1, g(p)=pa/(a−1)−a1​pa/(a−1)=aa−1​pa/(a−1)=bpb​,a1​+b1​=1,

since b≡a/(a−1)b\equiv a/(a-1)b≡a/(a−1) satisfies 1/b=(a−1)/a=1−1/a1/b = (a-1)/a = 1-1/a1/b=(a−1)/a=1−1/a. So Young's inequality reads px≤xa/a+pb/bpx\le x^{a}/a + p^{b}/bpx≤xa/a+pb/b, the inequality from which Hölder's and Minkowski's inequalities are built, and the reason conjugate exponents come in pairs summing to 111 in their reciprocals. Our worked example was a=4a=4a=4, b=4/3b=4/3b=4/3. ✓

What breaks without convexity. Take f(x)=14x4−12x2f(x)=\tfrac14x^{4}-\tfrac12x^{2}f(x)=41​x4−21​x2, the double well, which has f′′=3x2−1<0f''=3x^{2}-1\lt0f′′=3x2−1<0 on ∣x∣<1/3\abs{x}\lt1/\sqrt3∣x∣<1/3​. For each slope ppp there can now be three points with f′(x)=pf'(x)=pf′(x)=p, and (1.3.2) selects whichever gives the largest gap, the global one. The information about the other two is discarded, and the double transform g∗g^{*}g∗ comes back as the convex hull: the double well with its non-convex middle replaced by a straight segment. This is not a defect. It is exactly the Maxwell construction of a first-order phase transition: the flat segment is the coexistence region, the tie-line joining liquid and gas, and its slope is the common tangent, which is the shared value of the chemical potential. Legendre-transforming a non-convex free energy and getting a flat piece is the phase transition. Chapter 6.6 meets the same picture again with the Higgs potential.

The condition in nnn dimensions. With several variables, pi=∂f/∂xip_{i}=\partial f/\partial x^{i}pi​=∂f/∂xi is invertible for xxx precisely when the Jacobian of that map, the Hessian ∂2f/∂xi∂xj\partial^{2}f/\partial x^{i}\partial x^{j}∂2f/∂xi∂xj, is nonsingular, by the inverse function theorem of Chapter 0.6. Strict convexity in the multivariable sense means the Hessian is positive definite (Chapter 0.5), which is more than enough. Hold that thought. In §2 the Hessian in question is ∂2L/∂q˙i∂q˙j\partial^{2}L/\partial\dot q^{i}\partial\dot q^{j}∂2L/∂q˙​i∂q˙​j, which Chapter 1.2's grind box already showed is the positive-definite mass matrix whenever the kinetic energy is an honest quadratic form.

In plain terms 1.3.1

A curve can be given by listing its points, or by listing all the straight lines that graze it without crossing, and the two lists carry the same information, because a curve bending only one way is the highest of its own tangent lines. Swapping between the two descriptions is a standard operation, and performing it twice returns you exactly to where you began.

Which description you want is decided by what you are able to set. A laboratory has thermometers and no entropy meters, so a chemist labels a state by its temperature, which is the slope of the internal energy against entropy rather than the entropy itself, and the free energies are that one swap performed on one slot or another. What makes it reversible is that the curve bends one way only. Where it does not, the swap flattens the offending stretch permanently, and that flat stretch is a first-order phase transition rather than a defect in the mathematics.

In mechanics the variable traded away is the velocity and the slope accepted in its place is the momentum, and the reversibility condition becomes the statement that the kinetic energy is an honest positive quantity in the velocities. What the trade produces has been met before, as the combination a problem with no explicit clock in it happens to conserve.

2 · Momentum and the Hamiltonian

2.1 · The canonical momentum is not mvm\vv vmv

Before we transform anything, we need to be clear about the variable we are trading for. Chapter 1.2 defined, for any Lagrangian and any coordinates,

pi  ≡  ∂L∂q˙i, p_{i} \;\equiv\; \pdv{L}{\dot q^{i}}, pi​≡∂q˙​i∂L​, (1.3.11)

the canonical momentum conjugate to qiq^{i}qi, and noted that this makes the Euler–Lagrange equation read p˙i=∂L/∂qi\dot p_{i}=\partial L/\partial q^{i}p˙​i​=∂L/∂qi. In Cartesian coordinates with L=12mx˙2−V(x)L=\half m\dot{\vv x}^{2}-V(\vv x)L=21​mx˙2−V(x), (1.3.11) returns mx˙im\dot x^{i}mx˙i, which is why the name is not absurd. But that agreement is a special case, and it fails in two different ways that both matter.

It need not have the dimensions of momentum. For the pendulum with coordinate θ\thetaθ, L=12mℓ2θ˙2+mgℓcos⁡θL=\half m\ell^{2}\dot\theta^{2}+mg\ell\cos\thetaL=21​mℓ2θ˙2+mgℓcosθ gives pθ=mℓ2θ˙p_{\theta}=m\ell^{2}\dot\thetapθ​=mℓ2θ˙. That is an angular momentum, with units of J s\mathrm{J\,s}Js rather than kg m s−1\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}kgms−1. The word "conjugate" is the point. Whatever pip_{i}pi​ turns out to be, it is the thing that pairs with qiq^{i}qi so that pi dqip_{i}\,\dd q^{i}pi​dqi has the dimensions of action. Chapter 4.9's uncertainty relation Δq Δp≥ℏ/2\Delta q\,\Delta p\ge\hbar/2ΔqΔp≥ℏ/2 is dimensionally consistent for every conjugate pair for exactly this reason.

It need not be mvm\vv vmv even in Cartesian coordinates. This is the one worth being careful about, and seeing it costs one example. Chapter 2.6 will derive, from relativity, that a particle of charge eee in an electromagnetic field described by the scalar potential ϕ\phiϕ and vector potential A\vv AA has the Lagrangian

L  =  12m v⋅v  −  e ϕ(x,t)  +  e v⋅A(x,t). L \;=\; \half m\,\vv v\cdot\vv v \;-\; e\,\phi(\vv x,t) \;+\; e\,\vv v\cdot\vv A(\vv x,t). L=21​mv⋅v−eϕ(x,t)+ev⋅A(x,t). (1.3.12)

Worked example 1 checks that this reproduces the Lorentz force, so it is the right Lagrangian. Our question is what its canonical momentum is, so apply (1.3.11) to it, component by component, remembering that A\vv AA depends on position but not on velocity:

pi  =  ∂∂vi[12m vjvj+e vjAj]  =  mvi+eAi⟺p  =  mv+eA. p_{i} \;=\; \pdv{}{v^{i}}\left[\half m\,v^{j}v^{j} + e\,v^{j}A_{j}\right] \;=\; m v^{i} + e A_{i} \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad \vv p \;=\; m\vv v + e\vv A. pi​=∂vi∂​[21​mvjvj+evjAj​]=mvi+eAi​⟺p=mv+eA. (1.3.13)

The canonical momentum and the mechanical momentum mvm\vv vmv differ by eAe\vv AeA. This is the first time the vector potential has entered mechanics in this book, and it will not leave. Chapter 2.6 shows that A\vv AA is the spatial part of a four-vector AμA^{\mu}Aμ and that Maxwell's equations are its equations of motion. Chapter 6.3 shows that the entire structure of the Standard Model follows from demanding that the substitution p→p−eA\vv p\to\vv p - e\vv Ap→p−eA be forced on you by a symmetry principle. The name for that substitution is minimal coupling, and you have just watched it appear, three parts early, as an unremarkable partial derivative.

⚠ Why this isn't obvious

It is tempting to file (1.3.13) under "notation", on the grounds that mvm\vv vmv must be the real momentum and p\vv pp a bookkeeping device. That is exactly backwards, and the difference is measurable. Here is why it matters in practice.

The gauge problem. Chapter 1.2's Problem 4 showed that A→A+∇χ\vv A\to\vv A+\nabla\chiA→A+∇χ, ϕ→ϕ−∂tχ\phi\to\phi-\partial_{t}\chiϕ→ϕ−∂t​χ changes LLL by a total time derivative and therefore changes no physics. But it does change p\vv pp, by e∇χe\nabla\chie∇χ. So the canonical momentum is gauge-dependent, and by itself it is not an observable. Meanwhile mv=p−eAm\vv v = \vv p - e\vv Amv=p−eA is gauge-invariant, because A\vv AA shifts by exactly the same amount. The mechanical momentum is what you measure. The canonical momentum is what the formalism runs on. Both are needed and they are not the same object.

And yet it is p\vv pp that gets quantised. In Chapter 4.6 the operator conjugate to position is p^=−iℏ∇\hat{\vv p}=-\ii\hbar\nablap^​=−iℏ∇, and the rule for which classical quantity it represents is fixed by the bracket {qi,pj}=δji\{q^{i},p_{j}\}=\delta^{i}_{j}{qi,pj​}=δji​ of §6, which is a statement about the canonical momentum. Feed (1.3.13) into a Hamiltonian and the kinetic term becomes (p^−eA)2/2m(\hat{\vv p}-e\vv A)^{2}/2m(p^​−eA)2/2m, so that −iℏ∇-\ii\hbar\nabla−iℏ∇ is replaced by −iℏ∇−eA-\ii\hbar\nabla-e\vv A−iℏ∇−eA acting on the wavefunction. Every magnetic effect in quantum mechanics comes out of that one replacement: Landau levels, the Aharonov–Bohm phase, the Zeeman effect, superconducting flux quantisation. None of them would, if mvm\vv vmv were the thing you quantised.

⚑ The sharpest experimental statement is quoted forward to Chapter 6.3. In the Aharonov–Bohm effect an electron beam is split around a solenoid and recombined. Outside the solenoid the magnetic field is exactly zero, so a particle described by mvm\vv vmv alone can feel nothing. The interference fringes nonetheless shift, by an amount e∮A⋅dℓ/ℏe\oint\vv A\cdot\dd\vv\ell/\hbare∮A⋅dℓ/ℏ, which is the enclosed flux in units of ℏ/e\hbar/eℏ/e. The potential is not a computational convenience. It is where the physics lives, and p=mv+eA\vv p = m\vv v + e\vv Ap=mv+eA is the first hint.

2.2 · The Hamiltonian

Now we have both halves of the trade: a function LLL that depends on velocity, and a slope p=∂L/∂q˙p=\partial L/\partial\dot qp=∂L/∂q˙​ we would rather use instead. So perform §1's transform on LLL, taking q˙i\dot q^{i}q˙​i as the variable and holding qqq and ttt fixed. The conjugate slope is pi=∂L/∂q˙ip_{i}=\partial L/\partial\dot q^{i}pi​=∂L/∂q˙​i by (1.3.11), and the transform (1.3.4) reads

  H(q,p,t)  ≡  ∑ipi q˙i  −  L(q,q˙,t),   \boxed{\;H(q,p,t) \;\equiv\; \sum_{i}p_{i}\,\dot q^{i} \;-\; L\big(q,\dot q,t\big),\;} H(q,p,t)≡i∑​pi​q˙​i−L(q,q˙​,t),​ (1.3.14)

Every q˙i\dot q^{i}q˙​i on the right is to be eliminated in favour of the pip_{i}pi​ by inverting (1.3.11), and that instruction is the entire content of the definition. The result is a function of qqq, ppp and ttt only. This object is the Hamiltonian. Compare it with (1.3.1) and you can see that Chapter 1.2's Problem 2 was computing it: the conserved quantity of a time-independent Lagrangian is the Hamiltonian.

The inversion step is not free, and §1 told us exactly what it needs. Solving pi=∂L/∂q˙ip_{i}=\partial L/\partial\dot q^{i}pi​=∂L/∂q˙​i for q˙\dot qq˙​ requires that the map from velocities to momenta be invertible, and by the inverse function theorem that means asking about the Hessian

Wij  ≡  ∂2L∂q˙i ∂q˙j W_{ij} \;\equiv\; \frac{\partial^{2}L}{\partial\dot q^{i}\,\partial\dot q^{j}} Wij​≡∂q˙​i∂q˙​j∂2L​ (1.3.15)

which must be nonsingular. Chapter 1.2's grind box on the double pendulum established that when the coordinate change from Cartesians is time-independent, T=12∑ijMij(q)q˙iq˙jT=\half\sum_{ij}M_{ij}(q)\dot q^{i}\dot q^{j}T=21​∑ij​Mij​(q)q˙​iq˙​j with MMM symmetric positive definite, so W=MW=MW=M and the condition holds automatically.

⚑ It does not always hold, and the failure has a name. When LLL is linear in some velocity, the corresponding row of WWW vanishes, the transform is not invertible, and the system is called constrained. Dirac built a whole formalism for that case. It is quoted here and not developed, but you should know where it lives, because it is not an exotic corner. Gauge theories are there (Chapter 6.3: the Lagrangian of electromagnetism has no A˙0\dot A_{0}A˙0​ at all), and so is the reparametrisation-invariant string action (Chapter 7.2). Every fundamental theory in Parts VI and VII is a constrained system. So the honest statement is this. The clean Legendre transform of this section is the easy case, and it is the one that teaches you what the hard case is deforming.

2.3 · When H=T+VH=T+VH=T+V, and when it isn't

You have surely been told that the Hamiltonian is the total energy. It often is. But that is a theorem rather than a definition, and the theorem has two hypotheses that fail in ordinary situations. Let's state it, prove it, and then break it.

Theorem

Suppose (i) VVV does not depend on the velocities, and (ii) TTT is a homogeneous quadratic form in the generalised velocities, T=12∑ijMij(q)q˙iq˙jT=\half\sum_{ij}M_{ij}(q)\dot q^{i}\dot q^{j}T=21​∑ij​Mij​(q)q˙​iq˙​j. Then H=T+VH = T+VH=T+V.

Proof. With L=T−VL=T-VL=T−V and hypothesis (i), pi=∂L/∂q˙i=∂T/∂q˙ip_{i}=\partial L/\partial\dot q^{i} = \partial T/\partial\dot q^{i}pi​=∂L/∂q˙​i=∂T/∂q˙​i. Hypothesis (ii) says TTT is homogeneous of degree 222: replacing every q˙\dot qq˙​ by λq˙\lambda\dot qλq˙​ multiplies TTT by λ2\lambda^{2}λ2. What we want is the combination ∑piq˙i\sum p_{i}\dot q^{i}∑pi​q˙​i, so differentiate that homogeneity identity T(q,λq˙)=λ2T(q,q˙)T(q,\lambda\dot q) = \lambda^{2}T(q,\dot q)T(q,λq˙​)=λ2T(q,q˙​) with respect to λ\lambdaλ and set λ=1\lambda=1λ=1. The chain rule gives

∑iq˙i ∂T∂q˙i  =  2 T \sum_{i}\dot q^{i}\,\pdv{T}{\dot q^{i}} \;=\; 2\,T i∑​q˙​i∂q˙​i∂T​=2T (1.3.16)

which is Euler's theorem on homogeneous functions, derived rather than quoted. (The grind box does the general degree.) That is the whole input. Feed it into the definition of HHH and every term is now known:

H  =  ∑ipiq˙i−L  =  ∑iq˙i∂T∂q˙i−(T−V)  =  2T−T+V  =  T+V. H \;=\; \sum_{i}p_{i}\dot q^{i} - L \;=\; \sum_{i}\dot q^{i}\pdv{T}{\dot q^{i}} - (T-V) \;=\; 2T - T + V \;=\; T+V. H=i∑​pi​q˙​i−L=i∑​q˙​i∂q˙​i∂T​−(T−V)=2T−T+V=T+V. (1.3.17)

■\blacksquare■

Now let's break the hypotheses, using a system Chapter 1.2 already built. Problem 3 there put a bead on a hoop of radius RRR spun about its vertical diameter at a rate Ω\OmegaΩ fixed by a motor, and found

L  =  12mR2θ˙2  +  12mR2Ω2sin⁡2θ  +  mgRcos⁡θ. L \;=\; \half mR^{2}\dot\theta^{2} \;+\; \half mR^{2}\Omega^{2}\sin^{2}\theta \;+\; mgR\cos\theta. L=21​mR2θ˙2+21​mR2Ω2sin2θ+mgRcosθ. (1.3.18)

The middle term is part of the kinetic energy, since it is the speed the bead has purely because the hoop is carrying it around. But it contains no θ˙\dot\thetaθ˙. So TTT is not homogeneous of degree 222 in the velocity, and hypothesis (ii) fails. The theorem is therefore unavailable, and we must compute honestly instead. Since pθ=mR2θ˙p_{\theta}=mR^{2}\dot\thetapθ​=mR2θ˙, we have θ˙=pθ/mR2\dot\theta = p_{\theta}/mR^{2}θ˙=pθ​/mR2, and putting that into the definition gives HHH alongside the true energy for comparison:

H=pθθ˙−L  =  pθ22mR2  −  12mR2Ω2sin⁡2θ  −  mgRcos⁡θ,T+V=pθ22mR2  +  12mR2Ω2sin⁡2θ  −  mgRcos⁡θ. \begin{aligned} H &= p_{\theta}\dot\theta - L \;=\; \frac{p_{\theta}^{2}}{2mR^{2}} \;-\; \half mR^{2}\Omega^{2}\sin^{2}\theta \;-\; mgR\cos\theta,\\[4pt] T+V &= \frac{p_{\theta}^{2}}{2mR^{2}} \;+\; \half mR^{2}\Omega^{2}\sin^{2}\theta \;-\; mgR\cos\theta. \end{aligned} HT+V​=pθ​θ˙−L=2mR2pθ2​​−21​mR2Ω2sin2θ−mgRcosθ,=2mR2pθ2​​+21​mR2Ω2sin2θ−mgRcosθ.​ (1.3.19)

They differ by mR2Ω2sin⁡2θmR^{2}\Omega^{2}\sin^{2}\thetamR2Ω2sin2θ, which changes as the bead slides. HHH is conserved, since it has no explicit ttt. T+VT+VT+V is not, because the motor is doing work to hold Ω\OmegaΩ fixed. Conserved and "the energy" are different predicates, and HHH is the first one.

Notice also what HHH is here. It is the kinetic energy of the θ\thetaθ motion plus the effective potential VeffV_{\text{eff}}Veff​ that Chapter 1.2 found. The centrifugal term has flipped sign on its way through the transform and become part of the potential. That is not sleight of hand. It is (1.3.16) refusing to apply to a degree-zero term.

Grind box — Euler's theorem in general, the three-piece decomposition, and the relativistic particle

Euler's theorem. Let FFF be homogeneous of degree kkk in the variables uiu^{i}ui, meaning F(λu)=λkF(u)F(\lambda u) = \lambda^{k}F(u)F(λu)=λkF(u) for all λ>0\lambda \gt 0λ>0. Differentiate both sides with respect to λ\lambdaλ using the chain rule:

∑iui ∂F∂ui∣λu=k λk−1F(u), \sum_{i}u^{i}\,\pdv{F}{u^{i}}\bigg|_{\lambda u} = k\,\lambda^{k-1}F(u), i∑​ui∂ui∂F​​λu​=kλk−1F(u),

and set λ=1\lambda=1λ=1 to get ∑iui∂F/∂ui=kF\sum_{i}u^{i}\partial F/\partial u^{i} = kF∑i​ui∂F/∂ui=kF. That is the whole proof. Degree 222 gives (1.3.16), degree 111 gives ∑ui∂iF=F\sum u^{i}\partial_{i}F = F∑ui∂i​F=F, and degree 000 gives ∑ui∂iF=0\sum u^{i}\partial_{i}F = 0∑ui∂i​F=0.

The general Lagrangian. Split L=L2+L1+L0L = L_{2}+L_{1}+L_{0}L=L2​+L1​+L0​ by degree in q˙\dot qq˙​. Then piq˙i=2L2+L1p_{i}\dot q^{i} = 2L_{2}+L_{1}pi​q˙​i=2L2​+L1​ by the three cases above, so

H  =  (2L2+L1)−(L2+L1+L0)  =  L2−L0. H \;=\; \big(2L_{2}+L_{1}\big) - \big(L_{2}+L_{1}+L_{0}\big) \;=\; L_{2}-L_{0}. H=(2L2​+L1​)−(L2​+L1​+L0​)=L2​−L0​.

Every degree-one piece drops out of HHH entirely. Three consequences, all checkable against what we have already done:

  • Ordinary mechanics: L2=TL_{2}=TL2​=T, L1=0L_{1}=0L1​=0, L0=−VL_{0}=-VL0​=−V, giving H=T+VH=T+VH=T+V. ✓
  • Rotating hoop: L2=12mR2θ˙2L_{2}=\half mR^{2}\dot\theta^{2}L2​=21​mR2θ˙2, L1=0L_{1}=0L1​=0, L0=12mR2Ω2sin⁡2θ+mgRcos⁡θL_{0}=\half mR^{2}\Omega^{2}\sin^{2}\theta+mgR\cos\thetaL0​=21​mR2Ω2sin2θ+mgRcosθ, giving exactly (1.3.19). ✓ The centrifugal term's sign flip is the minus in L2−L0L_{2}-L_{0}L2​−L0​.
  • Charged particle: L2=12mv2L_{2}=\half mv^{2}L2​=21​mv2, L1=e v⋅AL_{1}=e\,\vv v\cdot\vv AL1​=ev⋅A, L0=−eϕL_{0}=-e\phiL0​=−eϕ, giving H=12mv2+eϕH = \half mv^{2}+e\phiH=21​mv2+eϕ. The magnetic term vanishes from HHH, which is the statement that magnetic forces do no work, derived rather than asserted. It reappears the moment you express HHH in terms of p\vv pp rather than v\vv vv, because 12mv2=(p−eA)2/2m\half mv^{2}=(\vv p-e\vv A)^{2}/2m21​mv2=(p−eA)2/2m. Worked example 1 does this properly.

The relativistic free particle. Chapter 1.2's table listed S=−mc2 ⁣∫dτS=-mc^{2}\!\int\dd\tauS=−mc2∫dτ, i.e. in one dimension L=−mc21−x˙2/c2L = -mc^{2}\sqrt{1-\dot x^{2}/c^{2}}L=−mc21−x˙2/c2​, which is not of the form T−VT-VT−V and is not homogeneous of any degree. Turn the crank anyway:

p=∂L∂x˙=−mc2⋅−x˙/c21−x˙2/c2=mx˙1−x˙2/c2=γmx˙. p = \pdv{L}{\dot x} = -mc^{2}\cdot\frac{-\dot x/c^{2}}{\sqrt{1-\dot x^{2}/c^{2}}} = \frac{m\dot x}{\sqrt{1-\dot x^{2}/c^{2}}} = \gamma m\dot x. p=∂x˙∂L​=−mc2⋅1−x˙2/c2​−x˙/c2​=1−x˙2/c2​mx˙​=γmx˙.

Then, using 1/γ=1−x˙2/c21/\gamma = \sqrt{1-\dot x^{2}/c^{2}}1/γ=1−x˙2/c2​,

H=px˙−L=γmx˙2+mc2γ=m(γ2x˙2+c2)γ=mc2γ2γ=γmc2, H = p\dot x - L = \gamma m\dot x^{2} + \frac{mc^{2}}{\gamma} = \frac{m\big(\gamma^{2}\dot x^{2}+c^{2}\big)}{\gamma} = \frac{mc^{2}\gamma^{2}}{\gamma} = \gamma mc^{2}, H=px˙−L=γmx˙2+γmc2​=γm(γ2x˙2+c2)​=γmc2γ2​=γmc2,

where the middle step used γ2x˙2+c2=c2γ2(x˙2/c2+1/γ2)=c2γ2\gamma^{2}\dot x^{2}+c^{2} = c^{2}\gamma^{2}\big(\dot x^{2}/c^{2}+1/\gamma^{2}\big) = c^{2}\gamma^{2}γ2x˙2+c2=c2γ2(x˙2/c2+1/γ2)=c2γ2. So H=γmc2H=\gamma mc^{2}H=γmc2, the relativistic energy including the rest energy, produced by a Legendre transform and nothing else. Expressed in the right variable, which is what HHH demands, we use p2c2=γ2m2x˙2c2p^{2}c^{2}=\gamma^{2}m^{2}\dot x^{2}c^{2}p2c2=γ2m2x˙2c2 and the same identity to get

H(p)=p2c2+m2c4. H(p) = \sqrt{p^{2}c^{2}+m^{2}c^{4}}. H(p)=p2c2+m2c4​.

That is the relation Chapter 2.5 derives from four-vectors and Chapter 5.5 quantises into the Dirac equation. It fell out of §1's transform applied to a square root. Note in passing that ∂2L/∂x˙2=mγ3>0\partial^{2}L/\partial\dot x^{2} = m\gamma^{3} \gt 0∂2L/∂x˙2=mγ3>0, so the Hessian condition (1.3.15) holds and the transform is legitimate. It is the same positivity Chapter 1.2's second-variation grind box used to show that a relativistic worldline maximises proper time.

In plain terms 1.3.2

The quantity paired with a coordinate here is not always mass times velocity, and the two ways it can differ both matter. For a pendulum described by an angle it is an angular momentum, with the wrong units for a momentum entirely, because what the pairing requires is that coordinate and partner multiply to something with the units of action. For a charge in a magnetic field it is not the mechanical momentum even in Cartesian coordinates, the field's potential having been added to it.

That second case is not notation. The mechanical momentum is what an instrument reads, while the conjugate one shifts when the potential is rewritten in a way that changes no physics, so the conjugate one is not by itself observable. Yet the conjugate one is what quantum mechanics turns into an operator, which is why every magnetic effect in that subject, including the interference shift around a solenoid whose field the electrons never enter, follows from a single substitution.

The other object built here is usually introduced as the total energy. It is the total energy under two hypotheses, both of which fail in ordinary situations, and a bead on a motor-driven hoop is enough to break them. The conserved quantity and the energy come apart there, and it is the first that the formulation runs on.

3 · Hamilton's equations, derived

We have a new function H(q,p,t)H(q,p,t)H(q,p,t). We do not yet have equations of motion in terms of it. There are two ways to get them, and they are worth seeing both, because they emphasise different things.

3.1 · First route: take the differential

Chapter 0.6's total differential is the statement that for any smooth function of several variables, the first-order change is the sum of the partial derivatives times the changes in their arguments. Our aim is to find out which variables HHH genuinely depends on, so apply that rule to the right-hand side of (1.3.14), treating qqq, q˙\dot qq˙​ and ttt as the independent variables there:

dH=∑i(q˙i dpi+pi dq˙i)  −  ∑i(∂L∂qidqi+∂L∂q˙i dq˙i)−∂L∂t dt. \begin{aligned} \dd H &= \sum_{i}\Big(\dot q^{i}\,\dd p_{i} + p_{i}\,\dd\dot q^{i}\Big) \;-\; \sum_{i}\left(\pdv{L}{q^{i}}\dd q^{i} + \pdv{L}{\dot q^{i}}\,\dd\dot q^{i}\right) - \pdv{L}{t}\,\dd t. \end{aligned} dH​=i∑​(q˙​idpi​+pi​dq˙​i)−i∑​(∂qi∂L​dqi+∂q˙​i∂L​dq˙​i)−∂t∂L​dt.​ (1.3.20)

Now look at the two terms containing dq˙i\dd\dot q^{i}dq˙​i. Their coefficients are pip_{i}pi​ and −∂L/∂q˙i-\partial L/\partial\dot q^{i}−∂L/∂q˙​i, and by the definition (1.3.11) those are equal and opposite. They cancel identically.

That cancellation is the entire trick, and it deserves a sentence of its own: the Legendre transform is engineered so that the variable you are trying to get rid of drops out of the differential. It is the same cancellation as (1.3.5), and the same one as dF=dU−TdS−SdT\dd F = \dd U - T\dd S - S\dd TdF=dU−TdS−SdT in the thermodynamics callout. Not an analogy. One theorem, appearing for the third time.

With those two terms gone, what survives is

dH  =  ∑iq˙i dpi  −  ∑i∂L∂qi dqi  −  ∂L∂t dt, \dd H \;=\; \sum_{i}\dot q^{i}\,\dd p_{i} \;-\; \sum_{i}\pdv{L}{q^{i}}\,\dd q^{i} \;-\; \pdv{L}{t}\,\dd t, dH=i∑​q˙​idpi​−i∑​∂qi∂L​dqi−∂t∂L​dt, (1.3.21)

which contains only dq\dd qdq, dp\dd pdp and dt\dd tdt. That confirms HHH really is a function of (q,p,t)(q,p,t)(q,p,t) and not secretly of the velocities. And once we know that, we may write its differential a second way, straight from the definition of a partial derivative:

dH  =  ∑i∂H∂qi dqi  +  ∑i∂H∂pi dpi  +  ∂H∂t dt. \dd H \;=\; \sum_{i}\pdv{H}{q^{i}}\,\dd q^{i} \;+\; \sum_{i}\pdv{H}{p_{i}}\,\dd p_{i} \;+\; \pdv{H}{t}\,\dd t. dH=i∑​∂qi∂H​dqi+i∑​∂pi​∂H​dpi​+∂t∂H​dt. (1.3.22)

Two expressions for the same differential, in terms of the same independent increments. Their coefficients must therefore match one by one. Comparing dpi\dd p_{i}dpi​, then dqi\dd q^{i}dqi, then dt\dd tdt gives three identities:

∂H∂pi=q˙i,∂H∂qi=−∂L∂qi,∂H∂t=−∂L∂t. \pdv{H}{p_{i}} = \dot q^{i}, \qquad \pdv{H}{q^{i}} = -\pdv{L}{q^{i}}, \qquad \pdv{H}{t} = -\pdv{L}{t}. ∂pi​∂H​=q˙​i,∂qi∂H​=−∂qi∂L​,∂t∂H​=−∂t∂L​. (1.3.23)

Only the middle one still mentions LLL, and we want equations in HHH alone, so kill it with the Euler–Lagrange equation, which says ∂L/∂qi=ddt(∂L/∂q˙i)=p˙i\partial L/\partial q^{i} = \dv{}{t}\big(\partial L/\partial\dot q^{i}\big) = \dot p_{i}∂L/∂qi=dtd​(∂L/∂q˙​i)=p˙​i​. And there they are:

  q˙i  =  ∂H∂pi,p˙i  =  −∂H∂qi,∂H∂t  =  −∂L∂t.   \boxed{\;\dot q^{i} \;=\; \pdv{H}{p_{i}}, \qquad\qquad \dot p_{i} \;=\; -\pdv{H}{q^{i}}, \qquad\qquad \pdv{H}{t} \;=\; -\pdv{L}{t}.\;} q˙​i=∂pi​∂H​,p˙​i​=−∂qi∂H​,∂t∂H​=−∂t∂L​.​ (1.3.24)

Hamilton's equations. Count what happened. Our nnn second-order equations became 2n2n2n first-order ones. Nothing was gained or lost in information, because a second-order equation always splits into two first-order ones, and the standard way to do that is to call q˙\dot qq˙​ a new variable. What is special here is which new variable was chosen. Choosing p=∂L/∂q˙p=\partial L/\partial\dot qp=∂L/∂q˙​ rather than q˙\dot qq˙​ itself is what produces the near-symmetry of (1.3.24), and that symmetry is worth everything that follows.

One immediate dividend, free of charge. Suppose HHH has no explicit time dependence, and ask how HHH changes along a trajectory. The chain rule plus (1.3.24) answers in one line:

dHdt=∑i(∂H∂qiq˙i+∂H∂pip˙i)+∂H∂t=∑i(−p˙iq˙i+q˙ip˙i)+0  =  0. \dv{H}{t} = \sum_{i}\left(\pdv{H}{q^{i}}\dot q^{i} + \pdv{H}{p_{i}}\dot p_{i}\right) + \pdv{H}{t} = \sum_{i}\Big(-\dot p_{i}\dot q^{i} + \dot q^{i}\dot p_{i}\Big) + 0 \;=\; 0. dtdH​=i∑​(∂qi∂H​q˙​i+∂pi​∂H​p˙​i​)+∂t∂H​=i∑​(−p˙​i​q˙​i+q˙​ip˙​i​)+0=0. (1.3.25)

HHH is conserved, by cancellation between the two halves of (1.3.24). That is Chapter 1.2's Beltrami identity again, now in three lines instead of five. Notice which feature did the work. The minus sign that made the two equations not symmetric is precisely what made the cancellation happen. Remember that, because §5 and §6 are both that minus sign.

3.2 · Second route: vary the action in phase space

The first derivation used the Euler–Lagrange equation as an input. Here is a derivation that does not, and that treats qqq and ppp on an equal footing from the start.

Rearrange (1.3.14) as L=∑ipiq˙i−HL = \sum_i p_{i}\dot q^{i}-HL=∑i​pi​q˙​i−H and substitute it into the action. Then declare qi(t)q^{i}(t)qi(t) and pi(t)p_{i}(t)pi​(t) to be 2n2n2n independent functions, with no relation between them assumed. The object to be made stationary is

S[q,p]  =  ∫t1t2[∑ipi q˙i  −  H(q,p,t)]dt. S[q,p] \;=\; \int_{t_{1}}^{t_{2}}\left[\sum_{i}p_{i}\,\dot q^{i} \;-\; H(q,p,t)\right]\dd t. S[q,p]=∫t1​t2​​[i∑​pi​q˙​i−H(q,p,t)]dt. (1.3.26)

This is a functional on a space of paths in the 2n2n2n-dimensional space of (q,p)(q,p)(q,p), and we ask for its stationary points exactly as Chapter 1.2 did. So vary both: q→q+ϵηq\to q+\epsilon\etaq→q+ϵη, p→p+ϵξp\to p+\epsilon\xip→p+ϵξ. Note the asymmetry that is about to matter. In (1.3.26) the velocity q˙\dot qq˙​ appears and p˙\dot pp˙​ does not. Collecting the terms linear in ϵ\epsilonϵ,

δS=∫t1t2∑i[ξiq˙i+piη˙i−∂H∂qiηi−∂H∂piξi]dt. \delta S = \int_{t_{1}}^{t_{2}}\sum_{i}\left[\xi_{i}\dot q^{i} + p_{i}\dot\eta^{i} - \pdv{H}{q^{i}}\eta^{i} - \pdv{H}{p_{i}}\xi_{i}\right]\dd t. δS=∫t1​t2​​i∑​[ξi​q˙​i+pi​η˙​i−∂qi∂H​ηi−∂pi​∂H​ξi​]dt. (1.3.27)

Only one term carries a derivative of a variation, and Chapter 1.2's move three handles it. We integrate ∫piη˙i dt\int p_{i}\dot\eta^{i}\,\dd t∫pi​η˙​idt by parts to get [piηi]t1t2−∫p˙iηi dt\big[p_{i}\eta^{i}\big]_{t_{1}}^{t_{2}} - \int\dot p_{i}\eta^{i}\,\dd t[pi​ηi]t1​t2​​−∫p˙​i​ηidt, so that every remaining term carries η\etaη or ξ\xiξ as a plain factor. Collecting those coefficients separately,

δS=[∑ipiηi]t1t2+∫t1t2∑i[(q˙i−∂H∂pi)ξi  −  (p˙i+∂H∂qi)ηi]dt. \delta S = \Big[\textstyle\sum_i p_{i}\eta^{i}\Big]_{t_{1}}^{t_{2}} + \int_{t_{1}}^{t_{2}}\sum_{i}\left[\left(\dot q^{i}-\pdv{H}{p_{i}}\right)\xi_{i} \;-\; \left(\dot p_{i}+\pdv{H}{q^{i}}\right)\eta^{i}\right]\dd t. δS=[∑i​pi​ηi]t1​t2​​+∫t1​t2​​∑i​[(q˙​i−∂pi​∂H​)ξi​−(p˙​i​+∂qi∂H​)ηi]dt. (1.3.28)

Kill the boundary term by requiring ηi(t1)=ηi(t2)=0\eta^{i}(t_{1})=\eta^{i}(t_{2})=0ηi(t1​)=ηi(t2​)=0, which fixes the positions at both ends, as before. Note carefully that no condition on ξ\xiξ is needed. Since ppp never appears differentiated, it generates no boundary term and is free at the endpoints.

That is not a technicality, and it is worth saying what it buys. It says the natural boundary-value problem in phase space is "specify where you start and where you finish", not "specify the whole initial state". Chapter 5.6's path integral sums over paths with fixed endpoints, and it inherits exactly this asymmetry.

Now apply the fundamental lemma (Chapter 1.2 §3.4) twice, once with ξ\xiξ arbitrary and η=0\eta=0η=0, and once the other way round. Each bracket must vanish separately, which gives

q˙i−∂H∂pi=0,p˙i+∂H∂qi=0, \dot q^{i} - \pdv{H}{p_{i}} = 0, \qquad\qquad \dot p_{i} + \pdv{H}{q^{i}} = 0, q˙​i−∂pi​∂H​=0,p˙​i​+∂qi∂H​=0, (1.3.29)

and that is (1.3.24) again. The two derivations agree, as they must, and each tells you something the other does not. Route one tells you the equations are the Legendre transform of Euler–Lagrange. Route two tells you they are themselves a variational principle, one in which position and momentum are independent variables of equal status.

3.3 · The minus sign, and what it is the seed of

Stare at (1.3.24) until the near-symmetry bothers you. The equations for qqq and ppp are the same equation with q↔pq\leftrightarrow pq↔p, except for one minus sign. That asymmetry is irreducible. You cannot rescale it away, because rescaling p→−pp\to-pp→−p just moves the sign to the other equation.

Since we cannot remove it, the next best thing is to give it a home of its own where we can see exactly what it does. Start by stacking the coordinates into one list of 2n2n2n numbers,

z  =  (q1,…,qn, p1,…,pn), z \;=\; \big(q^{1},\dots,q^{n},\,p_{1},\dots,p_{n}\big), z=(q1,…,qn,p1​,…,pn​), (1.3.30)

so that a single letter zzz now names the whole state. The minus sign is a relation between the first half of that list and the second half, so it should live in a 2n×2n2n\times2n2n×2n matrix. Define

Ω  =  (0In−In0),ΩT=−Ω,Ω2=−I2n,det⁡Ω=1. \Omega \;=\; \begin{pmatrix} 0 & I_{n}\\ -I_{n} & 0\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \Omega^{\mathsf T} = -\Omega, \qquad \Omega^{2} = -I_{2n}, \qquad \det\Omega = 1. Ω=(0−In​​In​0​),ΩT=−Ω,Ω2=−I2n​,detΩ=1. (1.3.31)

with the three properties on the right all read straight off the block form. With that one matrix in hand, both halves of (1.3.24) collapse into a single line:

z˙  =  Ω ∇H,(∇H)a=∂H∂za. \dot z \;=\; \Omega\,\nabla H, \qquad \big(\nabla H\big)_{a} = \pdv{H}{z^{a}}. z˙=Ω∇H,(∇H)a​=∂za∂H​. (1.3.32)

Check it: the top block of Ω∇H\Omega\nabla HΩ∇H is +∂H/∂p+\partial H/\partial p+∂H/∂p and the bottom block is −∂H/∂q-\partial H/\partial q−∂H/∂q. ✓

Now read that line geometrically, because it explains a fact we have already proved algebraically. The gradient of HHH points uphill, at right angles to the level sets. Ω\OmegaΩ rotates that direction by a quarter turn. So the system moves along the level sets, which is why HHH is conserved. The flow is everywhere perpendicular to the gradient, by construction.

Ω\OmegaΩ is called the symplectic form, and the antisymmetry ΩT=−Ω\Omega^{\mathsf T}=-\OmegaΩT=−Ω is the minus sign, isolated. Compare it with the object that runs Chapter 3.3, the metric gμνg_{\mu\nu}gμν​, which is symmetric and measures lengths. A symplectic form measures oriented areas instead, and it is the reason phase space has a geometry at all.

Every structural fact in the rest of this chapter is a consequence of the antisymmetry of Ω\OmegaΩ: Liouville's theorem, the Poisson bracket, and the [q^,p^]=iℏ[\hat q,\hat p]=\ii\hbar[q^​,p^​]=iℏ of quantum mechanics. So is the fact that phase space is always even-dimensional. An antisymmetric matrix in odd dimensions has det⁡Ω=det⁡ΩT=det⁡(−Ω)=(−1)2n+1det⁡Ω\det\Omega = \det\Omega^{\mathsf T} = \det(-\Omega) = (-1)^{2n+1}\det\OmegadetΩ=detΩT=det(−Ω)=(−1)2n+1detΩ, forcing det⁡Ω=0\det\Omega=0detΩ=0, so no invertible Ω\OmegaΩ exists there.

In plain terms 1.3.3

Trading one second-order equation for two first-order ones is available to anybody and costs nothing, since calling the velocity a new variable does it. All of the content here is in which new variable was chosen. Taking the conjugate partner rather than the velocity produces two equations that are the same equation with the roles of coordinate and momentum exchanged, apart from a single minus sign sitting in one of them.

That sign cannot be removed. Reversing the sign of the momentum only moves it to the other equation, and it is what makes the two halves of the calculation cancel when you ask whether the energy changes, so that the energy does not change. Written compactly the sign becomes an antisymmetric object standing between the two halves of the space, whose effect is to turn a gradient through a quarter turn, so the motion runs along the level surfaces of the energy rather than across them.

Everything structural in the rest of the chapter is that antisymmetry and nothing else. A symmetric object of the same general kind measures lengths and will run the chapters on gravity; this one measures oriented areas instead, which is a different geometry and the reason the space must have an even number of dimensions, an antisymmetric table in an odd number of them being necessarily degenerate.

4 · Phase space

The space whose points are the 2n2n2n numbers z=(q,p)z=(q,p)z=(q,p) is phase space. Chapter 0.8 introduced it for the oscillator and promised it would come back. This is where it becomes the setting rather than a picture.

4.1 · One point fixes everything, and trajectories cannot cross

Hamilton's equations (1.3.32) are first order. That is the structural difference from the Lagrangian formulation, and it changes what a "state" is. Chapter 0.8's Picard–Lindelöf theorem says that a first-order system z˙=F(z)\dot z = F(z)z˙=F(z) with FFF Lipschitz has exactly one solution through each initial point. Applied here, that gives us the following.

The defining property of phase space

A single point of phase space determines the entire past and future of the system. Not a point plus a velocity. A point.

Configuration space does not have this property. A pendulum passing through θ=0\theta=0θ=0 might be moving left or right, fast or slow, so "θ=0\theta=0θ=0" is not a state. Phase space is precisely the space of things that are states, which is why Chapter 0.8 said the list the existence theorem asks for is the list phase space is made of.

There is an immediate geometric consequence, and it is what makes phase portraits legible.

Claim. If HHH has no explicit time dependence, two distinct trajectories can never cross.

Proof. Suppose the trajectory z1z_{1}z1​ passes through the point z∗z_{\ast}z∗​ at time t1t_{1}t1​ and the trajectory z2z_{2}z2​ passes through the same z∗z_{\ast}z∗​ at time t2t_{2}t2​. Because HHH does not depend on ttt, the right-hand side of (1.3.32) depends only on the point, so shifting a solution in time gives another solution. Define z~2(t)=z2(t+t2−t1)\tilde z_{2}(t) = z_{2}(t+t_{2}-t_{1})z~2​(t)=z2​(t+t2​−t1​), which also solves the equations and satisfies z~2(t1)=z∗\tilde z_{2}(t_{1}) = z_{\ast}z~2​(t1​)=z∗​. Now z1z_{1}z1​ and z~2\tilde z_{2}z~2​ are two solutions with the same value at t1t_{1}t1​, so by uniqueness they are the same solution. Hence z2z_{2}z2​ is z1z_{1}z1​ retimed, and it is the same curve. ■\blacksquare■

So through every point of phase space there passes exactly one curve, and phase space is filled by these curves like the streamlines of a steady fluid, with no branching, no merging and no intersections. The only points where curves appear to meet are fixed points, where ∇H=0\nabla H=0∇H=0 and the "trajectory" is a single stationary point. We will meet one shortly.

4.2 · The harmonic oscillator, again

The quickest way to get a feel for a flow is to draw one we already know. Take H=p22m+12mω2q2H = \dfrac{p^{2}}{2m} + \half m\omega^{2}q^{2}H=2mp2​+21​mω2q2, which is T+VT+VT+V, since both hypotheses of §2.3 hold. Differentiating it in ppp and in qqq gives Hamilton's equations for the oscillator:

q˙=∂H∂p=pm,p˙=−∂H∂q=−mω2q. \dot q = \pdv{H}{p} = \frac{p}{m}, \qquad\qquad \dot p = -\pdv{H}{q} = -m\omega^{2}q. q˙​=∂p∂H​=mp​,p˙​=−∂q∂H​=−mω2q. (1.3.33)

The first says p=mq˙p=m\dot qp=mq˙​, recovering the mechanical momentum. Substituting it into the second gives mq¨=−mω2qm\ddot q = -m\omega^{2}qmq¨​=−mω2q, the oscillator equation. Nothing new so far. But now read the pair as a flow instead of as a route back to a second-order equation.

The level sets of HHH are the ellipses of Chapter 0.8 §4.4, and by §3.3 the motion runs along them. To see what the motion actually is, we would like the ellipses to be circles, so rescale the two axes by equal and opposite factors:

Q  =  mω  q,P  =  pmω, Q \;=\; \sqrt{m\omega}\;q, \qquad\qquad P \;=\; \frac{p}{\sqrt{m\omega}}, Q=mω​q,P=mω​p​, (1.3.34)

which has the virtue of preserving areas, since dQ dP=dq dp\dd Q\,\dd P = \dd q\,\dd pdQdP=dqdp. That is a property §8 will name. In these variables H=ω2(P2+Q2)H = \tfrac{\omega}{2}\big(P^{2}+Q^{2}\big)H=2ω​(P2+Q2), and rewriting (1.3.33) in them gives

Q˙  =  ωP,P˙  =  −ωQ. \dot Q \;=\; \omega P, \qquad\qquad \dot P \;=\; -\omega Q. Q˙​=ωP,P˙=−ωQ. (1.3.35)

That is a rigid rotation of the whole plane at angular velocity ω\omegaω, clockwise. Every point, whatever its energy, goes round at the same rate, which is the phase-space statement of the fact that a harmonic oscillator's period is independent of amplitude. Chapter 0.1 observed that i\iii is a rotation by 90°. Here the rotation is generated by Ω\OmegaΩ, which squares to −1-1−1 for the same reason. The oscillator flow is multiplication by e−iωt\ee^{-\ii\omega t}e−iωt, drawn.

4.3 · The pendulum, and the separatrix

Now a system where the flow is not uniform. Take the pendulum of Chapter 1.2 §6.2, with q=θq=\thetaq=θ and p=mℓ2θ˙p=m\ell^{2}\dot\thetap=mℓ2θ˙. Both hypotheses of §2.3 hold, so its Hamiltonian is the total energy:

H  =  p22mℓ2  +  mgℓ(1−cos⁡q), H \;=\; \frac{p^{2}}{2m\ell^{2}} \;+\; mg\ell\big(1-\cos q\big), H=2mℓ2p2​+mgℓ(1−cosq), (1.3.36)

where the constant has been chosen so that H=0H=0H=0 at the bottom. Hamilton's equations are q˙=p/mℓ2\dot q = p/m\ell^{2}q˙​=p/mℓ2 and p˙=−mgℓsin⁡q\dot p = -mg\ell\sin qp˙​=−mgℓsinq, reproducing q¨=−(g/ℓ)sin⁡q\ddot q = -(g/\ell)\sin qq¨​=−(g/ℓ)sinq. Write ω02=g/ℓ\omega_{0}^{2}=g/\ellω02​=g/ℓ.

Since HHH is conserved, trajectories are its level sets, and there are three kinds.

Libration. For 0<H<2mgℓ0 \lt H \lt 2mg\ell0<H<2mgℓ the bob cannot reach the top. Setting p=0p=0p=0 in (1.3.36) gives a turning point at cos⁡q=1−H/mgℓ\cos q = 1 - H/mg\ellcosq=1−H/mgℓ, which has a solution only when H≤2mgℓH\le2mg\ellH≤2mgℓ. The level set is a closed curve encircling the origin, and the motion is back-and-forth swinging. Near the origin, expanding 1−cos⁡q≈q2/21-\cos q\approx q^{2}/21−cosq≈q2/2 recovers the oscillator of §4.2 and the level curves are Chapter 0.8's ellipses.

Rotation. For H>2mgℓH \gt 2mg\ellH>2mgℓ there is no turning point. Here ppp never vanishes, so the bob goes over the top and keeps going. The level set is an open curve running across the whole range of qqq, and since qqq and q+2πq+2\piq+2π are the same physical configuration, phase space here is really a cylinder and the curve is a loop around it.

The separatrix. Between those two behaviours sits one energy at which the bob arrives at the inverted position q=πq=\piq=π with exactly zero momentum. Putting q=πq=\piq=π, p=0p=0p=0 into (1.3.36) gives its value:

Hsep  =  2mgℓ, H_{\text{sep}} \;=\; 2mg\ell, Hsep​=2mgℓ, (1.3.37)

We would like the curve itself, not only its energy, so solve (1.3.36) for ppp at this energy, using 1−cos⁡q=2sin⁡2(q/2)1-\cos q = 2\sin^{2}(q/2)1−cosq=2sin2(q/2) to make the square root come out cleanly:

p22mℓ2=mgℓ(1+cos⁡q)=2mgℓcos⁡2q2  ⟹  p=± 2mℓ2ω0cos⁡q2, \frac{p^{2}}{2m\ell^{2}} = mg\ell\big(1+\cos q\big) = 2mg\ell\cos^{2}\frac{q}{2} \;\Longrightarrow\; p = \pm\,2m\ell^{2}\omega_{0}\cos\frac{q}{2}, 2mℓ2p2​=mgℓ(1+cosq)=2mgℓcos22q​⟹p=±2mℓ2ω0​cos2q​, (1.3.38)

These are the two arcs Chapter 0.8 §8.2 found. They meet at q=±πq=\pm\piq=±π, p=0p=0p=0, and that meeting point is a fixed point, since ∂H/∂q=mgℓsin⁡π=0\partial H/\partial q = mg\ell\sin\pi = 0∂H/∂q=mgℓsinπ=0 and ∂H/∂p=0\partial H/\partial p=0∂H/∂p=0. So §4.1's no-crossing theorem is not violated. To see what the flow does near it, linearise by writing q=π+uq=\pi+uq=π+u, so that sin⁡q=−sin⁡u≈−u\sin q = -\sin u \approx -usinq=−sinu≈−u:

u˙=pmℓ2,p˙=+mgℓ u⟹u¨=+ω02 u, \dot u = \frac{p}{m\ell^{2}}, \qquad \dot p = +mg\ell\,u \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \ddot u = +\omega_{0}^{2}\,u, u˙=mℓ2p​,p˙​=+mgℓu⟹u¨=+ω02​u, (1.3.39)

whose solutions are e±ω0t\ee^{\pm\omega_{0}t}e±ω0​t, one growing and one decaying. This is a hyperbolic fixed point, or saddle. The level curves near it are hyperbolas, and the separatrix is the pair of straight lines they asymptote to. The decaying solution is the trajectory that creeps toward the inverted position and takes infinite time to arrive. The growing one is the same trajectory run backwards.

Compare the origin, where the same calculation gives u¨=−ω02u\ddot u = -\omega_{0}^{2}uu¨=−ω02​u and the level curves are closed. That is an elliptic fixed point, or centre. Two fixed points, two signs, two completely different local pictures, and the entire qualitative structure of the pendulum is the statement that they are joined by the separatrix.

4.4 · What the enclosed area means

For a closed orbit, meaning a libration, the natural number to attach to it is the area it encloses:

A(E)  =  ∮H=Ep dq, \mathcal{A}(E) \;=\; \oint_{H=E} p\,\dd q, A(E)=∮H=E​pdq, (1.3.40)

where the line integral around the closed curve equals the enclosed area by Green's theorem (Chapter 0.7 §5.1). That is what a line integral of p dqp\,\dd qpdq around a loop is. Two facts make this the right quantity to care about.

First: its derivative is the period. To see it, ask how the area responds when the energy changes. Solve H(q,p)=EH(q,p)=EH(q,p)=E for ppp on the upper branch and differentiate (1.3.40) under the integral sign. Since ∂p/∂E\partial p/\partial E∂p/∂E at fixed qqq is the reciprocal of ∂H/∂p\partial H/\partial p∂H/∂p at fixed qqq, and ∂H/∂p=q˙\partial H/\partial p = \dot q∂H/∂p=q˙​, the integrand turns into dt\dd tdt:

dAdE  =  ∮∂p∂E dq  =  ∮dq∂H/∂p  =  ∮dqq˙  =  ∮dt  =  T(E). \dv{\mathcal{A}}{E} \;=\; \oint\pdv{p}{E}\,\dd q \;=\; \oint\frac{\dd q}{\partial H/\partial p} \;=\; \oint\frac{\dd q}{\dot q} \;=\; \oint\dd t \;=\; T(E). dEdA​=∮∂E∂p​dq=∮∂H/∂pdq​=∮q˙​dq​=∮dt=T(E). (1.3.41)

The area is the antiderivative of the period. For the oscillator, Chapter 0.8 computed A=2πE/ω\mathcal{A}=2\pi E/\omegaA=2πE/ω, so dA/dE=2π/ω=T\dd\mathcal{A}/\dd E = 2\pi/\omega = TdA/dE=2π/ω=T ✓, and since TTT does not depend on EEE there, the area is exactly linear in the energy. For the pendulum it is not. Numerical integration of (1.3.40) at ω0=1\omega_{0}=1ω0​=1, mℓ2=1m\ell^{2}=1mℓ2=1 gives dA/dE=6.449765\dd\mathcal{A}/\dd E = 6.449765dA/dE=6.449765 at E=0.2E=0.2E=0.2 and 11.63334911.63334911.633349 at E=1.9E=1.9E=1.9, against periods 4K(E/2)/ω04K(E/2)/\omega_{0}4K(E/2)/ω0​ of 6.4497656.4497656.449765 and 11.63334911.63334911.633349 from Chapter 0.8's elliptic-integral formula. Agreement to ten digits, which is the sort of thing worth checking once.

Second: it is what quantum mechanics rations. ⚑ Quoted forward to Chapters 4.8 and 4.10. The Bohr–Sommerfeld condition states that in the semiclassical regime the allowed orbits are those with

∮p dq  =  (n+12)h,n=0,1,2,… \oint p\,\dd q \;=\; \left(n+\tfrac12\right)h, \qquad n=0,1,2,\dots ∮pdq=(n+21​)h,n=0,1,2,… (1.3.42)

with h=2πℏh=2\pi\hbarh=2πℏ Planck's constant. For the oscillator this reads 2πEn/ω=(n+12)h2\pi E_{n}/\omega = (n+\tfrac12)h2πEn​/ω=(n+21​)h, that is En=(n+12)ℏωE_{n}=(n+\tfrac12)\hbar\omegaEn​=(n+21​)ℏω, which Chapter 4.8 will derive exactly, with ladder operators and no semiclassical approximation, and get precisely this answer. That is the one case in which the condition is exact rather than semiclassical, and it is the only part of this flag 4.8 discharges. The general statement, and the measurement of how far it is from the truth when the potential is not a parabola, is Chapter 4.10 §6.

So the classical phase-space ellipse is not deleted by quantum mechanics. It is quantised. The continuum of orbits becomes a discrete stack of them, one per unit of hhh of enclosed area, and the ground state is the one with half a unit. Phase-space area is measured in units of Planck's constant. That sentence is the reason hhh has the units it does, namely J s\mathrm{J\,s}Js, the units of p dqp\,\dd qpdq, and it is the single most useful thing to remember about phase space.

Grind box — the area–period relation done carefully, and the adiabatic invariant

The derivation, without hand-waving. Take a one-dimensional system with H(q,p)H(q,p)H(q,p) and a closed orbit at energy EEE. On the upper half of the orbit write p=p+(q,E)p=p_{+}(q,E)p=p+​(q,E). The enclosed area is A(E)=∮p dq\mathcal{A}(E)=\oint p\,\dd qA(E)=∮pdq, traversed so the integral is positive. Differentiating with respect to EEE moves the curve. The endpoints, which are the turning points, move too, but p=0p=0p=0 there, so the boundary contribution vanishes and we may differentiate under the integral:

dAdE=∮(∂p∂E) ⁣qdq. \dv{\mathcal{A}}{E} = \oint\left(\pdv{p}{E}\right)_{\!q}\dd q. dEdA​=∮(∂E∂p​)q​dq.

Now, differentiating the identity H(q,p(q,E))=EH\big(q,p(q,E)\big) = EH(q,p(q,E))=E with respect to EEE at fixed qqq gives (∂H/∂p)(∂p/∂E)=1\big(\partial H/\partial p\big)\big(\partial p/\partial E\big) = 1(∂H/∂p)(∂p/∂E)=1, so ∂p/∂E=1/q˙\partial p/\partial E = 1/\dot q∂p/∂E=1/q˙​. Hence the integrand is dq/q˙=dt\dd q/\dot q = \dd tdq/q˙​=dt, and integrating once round the orbit gives one period. ■\blacksquare■

The action variable. Define J=A/2πJ = \mathcal{A}/2\piJ=A/2π. Then dE/dJ=2π/T=ω(E)\dd E/\dd J = 2\pi/T = \omega(E)dE/dJ=2π/T=ω(E), the angular frequency. Problem 3 constructs a change of variables in which JJJ is literally the new momentum and the new coordinate is an angle advancing uniformly at rate ω\omegaω. These are action–angle variables, and they turn any one-dimensional bound motion into the trivial system ϑ˙=ω\dot\vartheta=\omegaϑ˙=ω, J˙=0\dot J = 0J˙=0.

⚑ One quoted fact, because it explains why (1.3.42) was ever a sensible guess. If a parameter of the system (a pendulum's length, say) is changed slowly compared with the period, then EEE and TTT both change but JJJ does not, to all orders in the slowness. JJJ is an adiabatic invariant. Ehrenfest's argument was that only an adiabatic invariant can sensibly be quantised, since if you could change JJJ by gently stretching a wire you could move a system off its allowed levels without a transition, and that is how Bohr and Sommerfeld chose which quantity to set equal to nhnhnh. The modern statement is Chapter 4.17's adiabatic theorem: a quantum system stays in the nnn-th eigenstate under slow change, which is the same sentence with JJJ replaced by nnn.

EEEdA/dE\dd\mathcal{A}/\dd EdA/dE (numerical)T=4K(E/2)T=4K(E/2)T=4K(E/2)relative difference
